hook.text: Here's a URL shortener that works: a load balancer, two stateless app servers, a cache and a key-value store, sized for about thirty-five thousand redirects a second at peak.

hook-10x.text: Now give it ten times the traffic, three hundred and fifty thousand a second, and every box has to answer for it.

plan.text: Twelve questions: nine worked through on this diagram, two quick ones, and a news feed to close.

q1.text: Question one. Horizontal versus vertical scaling, which do you reach for? Vertical is a bigger machine: simple, but it has a ceiling, and it's still one machine that can fail.

q1-horiz.text: Horizontal is more machines behind the load balancer: nearly unlimited, and redundant, but only if any server can handle any request. So keep the app tier stateless, with session state in a shared cache or database.

q1-ours.text: These redirect servers already are, so ten times the traffic means more of them.

q1-headroom.text: How many more? Enough that none runs near full. In the simplest queue model, a request waits one service time on average at fifty percent load, nine at ninety percent, and ninety-nine at ninety-nine.

q1-buy.text: Headroom is what the extra servers buy.

q2.text: Question two. What is a load balancer, and how does it distribute traffic? It sits in front of the pool and spreads requests, so no one server is overwhelmed.

q2-algos.text: Round-robin deals them in turn. Least-connections picks the server with the fewest open connections, which copes with slow requests. Consistent hashing sends a key to the same server every time, for servers that cache their own hot links.

q2-health.text: And health checks pull a dead server out of rotation, which is what makes a pool of stateless servers highly available.

q2-mod.text: Why consistent? Simulate ten thousand short keys on three servers, by hash modulo three. Add a fourth, switch to modulo four, and seventy-four percent of the keys move, each one to a cold cache.

q2-ring.text: On a hash ring, with a hundred points a server, only twenty-three percent move, all of them to the new server.

q3.text: Question three. Explain the cache-aside pattern. On a read, the app checks the cache. On a miss, it reads the database, writes the value into the cache, and returns it. A write updates the database and invalidates the cached copy.

q3-props.text: Only what's asked for gets cached, and a cache failure falls through to the database, but every key's first request pays the miss.

q3-sim.text: Simulate two million redirects over a million links, where a few links get most of the clicks. A cache holding a thousandth of the links answers forty percent. A hundredth, fifty-eight. A tenth, seventy-seven.

q3-loss.text: And the better it works, the harder losing it lands: a dead cache multiplies the database's reads by two point four at fifty-eight percent, and by more than four at seventy-seven. So the cache needs replicas too.

q4.text: Question four. Why is cache invalidation hard? Because there are two copies of the truth, and they drift. Set the TTL, the time to live, too long and users see stale data; too short and you lose the cache's benefit.

q4-model.text: Take a simple model: a key read about once a second and changed every two minutes.

q4-ours.text: A short link barely changes, so its TTL can be long, until one is taken down for abuse. Then delete its cached entry after the database commits. Delete it first, and a read in between puts the old value back.

q4-write.text: Write-through updates both together, consistent at a cost on every write. Write-behind batches writes for speed, and a crash loses what it hadn't written.

q5.text: Question five. What is database replication, and what does it buy you? Copies of the data on several nodes. In leader-follower replication, writes go to the leader and stream to read-only followers. That scales reads, and if the leader dies, a follower is promoted.

q5-lag.text: The catch is replication lag. Someone creates a link and opens it at once, and the read lands on a follower that hasn't caught up: not found.

q5-fix.text: So for a short while after a user writes, send their reads to the leader. And with asynchronous replication, promoting a lagging follower loses the writes it never received.

q6.text: Question six. What is sharding, and how does it differ from partitioning? Partitioning splits one large table into pieces. Sharding puts the pieces on separate database servers, by a shard key, to scale writes and storage past one machine.

q6-key.text: Shard by creation date, and today's shard takes every new link: a hot spot. Shard by a hash of the short key, and in a simulation, a million keys land on eight shards within one percent of an eighth each.

q6-cost.text: A redirect touches one shard, but listing one user's links asks all eight: cross-shard queries are the price. Keep a second copy keyed by user for that page.

q7.text: Question seven. Explain the CAP theorem. During a network partition, a distributed system can't be both consistent, every read seeing the latest write, and available, every working node still answering. So each side either refuses, or answers and risks stale data.
q7.spoken: Question seven. Explain the cap theorem. During a network partition, a distributed system can't be both consistent, every read seeing the latest write, and available, every working node still answering. So each side either refuses, or answers and risks stale data.

q7-ours.text: It's a choice per operation, not a label for the database. A redirect answers from whatever copy it reaches; at worst, a brand-new link isn't found yet, or one just taken down still works. New keys can be minted on both sides, if each server draws from its own block of IDs. But a custom alias must be unique, so the side without a majority refuses it.

q7-pacelc.text: And on a healthy network, waiting for replicas to confirm a write still trades latency for consistency: the second half of PACELC.
q7-pacelc.spoken: And on a healthy network, waiting for replicas to confirm a write still trades latency for consistency: the second half of pass-elk.

q8.text: Question eight. When do you introduce a message queue? When work doesn't need to finish inside the request. Counting clicks in the database makes every redirect wait on a write, and sends a viral link's whole spike there.

q8-queue.text: Queue each click instead. The redirect returns at once, workers drain the queue at their own pace, and a burst just makes it longer. Slow work, like email or video transcoding, goes the same way.

q8-once.text: The price is at-least-once delivery: a worker that crashes before acknowledging gets the click again. So make the consumer idempotent: give each click an ID, and record the ID in the same transaction that adds to the count, so a repeat changes nothing. The totals now run a little behind.

q9.text: Question nine. How does rate limiting work? It caps a client's requests per window, to protect the system and keep it fair. Say ten new links a minute, and one client sends ten at fifty-nine seconds, then ten at sixty-one.

q9-fixed.text: A fixed-window counter resets on the minute, so all twenty get through: twice the limit, for one cheap counter.

q9-sliding.text: A sliding-window counter weighs in the minute before and refuses the second ten, though it's an estimate that assumes requests were evenly spread.

q9-token.text: A token bucket holds ten tokens and refills one every six seconds. Each request spends one, so a client that's been quiet can burst ten at once, and an empty bucket answers HTTP four twenty-nine, too many requests. Here the first burst empties it, and the second is refused.

q9-leaky.text: A leaky bucket queues requests and lets them out at a constant rate, one every six seconds, so the servers behind it see a smooth stream, and a burst waits its turn.

q9-shared.text: The follow-up is where the count lives. With four app servers, each keeping its own bucket, round-robin hands one client four buckets: four times the limit. The count belongs in a store they all share.

r-evict.text: When a cache fills, LRU, least recently used, drops the entry untouched longest: a good default. LFU, least frequently used, keeps popular keys through a quiet spell. First in, first out evicts in insertion order, used or not. And a TTL expires entries on a timer, bounding staleness whatever the memory pressure. Most systems pair LRU with a TTL.

r-consist.text: And the consistency models to know. Strong: every read reflects the latest write. Eventual: replicas converge once writes stop, and a read can be stale meanwhile. Between them, read-your-writes, the fix from question five, and monotonic reads, where you never see time go backwards. A feed can be eventual; a bank balance usually needs strong.

q12.text: Question twelve. Design a news feed: fan-out on write, or on read? Fan-out on write, or push, copies each new post's ID into every follower's precomputed feed, so reading one is a cheap lookup.

q12-storm.text: Its cost is per follower: two hundred followers, two hundred writes. A celebrity with fifty million followers makes fifty million writes from one post: a write storm.

q12-pull.text: Fan-out on read, or pull, builds the feed on request from everyone you follow. Posting is cheap, but follow three hundred accounts and every load reads three hundred timelines.

q12-why.text: Feeds are read far more often than people post, so push usually wins:

q12-hybrid.text: So real systems mix them: push for ordinary accounts, pull for celebrities, merged at read time. Follow five celebrities, and a load is six reads, not three hundred, and no post costs fifty million writes.

next.text: That's the design, grown for ten times the traffic.

next-api.text: Every box in it talks to the others through an API. Next: API design.

q4-cross.text: The least bad TTL is where the two failures cross, about fifteen seconds, and even there six percent of reads miss and six percent are stale.

q1-db.text: Vertical still has its place: the database holds the state, so it usually scales up first, until it nears that ceiling.

q2-clock.text: Each key belongs to the next point clockwise, so a new server's points take only the keys just before them.

q4-backstop.text: Even then, a slow read can race the delete, so the TTL stays as a backstop: it bounds how long a wrong value lives.

q5-sync.text: Semi-synchronous replication fixes that: each write waits until one follower has it, so promoting that follower loses nothing, but every write is slower.

q6-ring.text: Add a ninth shard and modulo moves eighty-nine percent of the keys; a hash ring, as in question two, moves thirteen percent.
